This is the source data that energy guarantees rest on. State plainly whether it is a contract commitment, a catalogue curve, or a curve measured at acceptance — three different things in law, and mixing them means that when a warranty claim comes, nobody knows what is being compared with what.

This is the metadata of the time-series store: what the point measures, in what unit, how it aggregates onto a chart, and what counts as an implausible figure. The readings themselves live in a separate table outside the ORM — a 12-tower plant sampled every minute produces over 300 million rows a year.

The rules here only raise a quality flag; they do NOT delete readings. Filter and then delete the original and it can never be proved again — and the retention requirement says plainly: do not delete, do not compress the originals lossily.

The control type decides WHAT is corrected. A pitch turbine normalises wind speed by the cube root of the density ratio; a stall turbine normalises power. Do it the other way round and the whole curve is wrong.

The aggregation may be wrong. Averaging a cumulative energy counter gives a meaningless number; averaging wind direction arithmetically points the OPPOSITE way (the mean of 350° and 10° is 180°); averaging a 0/1 state means nothing at all. This is the quietest mistake of all — the chart still looks smooth.

Mean turbulence intensity %(ti).1f%% — high. The binning method is SYSTEMATICALLY biased upwards in gusty wind, because the power curve is convex and so the mean power exceeds the power at the mean wind speed. The "exceeds the commitment" figure below may be a mathematical artefact rather than a good turbine. For a firm conclusion, normalise for turbulence per IEC 61400-12-1 edition 2, or compare against another turbine at the same plant over the same period.

Written with tag codes. Computed at READ time rather than stored, so changing the formula changes every past chart with it — a wrong formula has to be wrong everywhere, rather than leaving old figures computed by the old formula with nobody aware of it.
Any interval missing a source tag is DROPPED rather than replaced by 0: a 0 in the denominator gives infinity, and in the numerator a performance of 0 that looks like a real fault.

An exclusion period is quite different from a quality flag. A quality flag says this reading may be WRONG. An exclusion period says the reading is entirely RIGHT, but this period does not count towards KPIs — a turbine under planned maintenance rightly produces zero energy, and counting that in the availability factor penalises the plant for doing exactly what it should.
The raw readings are untouched: the exclusion is applied at read time, so correcting the reason later makes every indicator recompute correctly at once.
